founded.what: The year three partners founded the house at Aÿ, on 6 February by the trade union's chronology, under the name Renaudin Bollinger.

place: Aÿ, Vallée de la Marne, Champagne

kind.means: A négociant manipulant, a house in the trade's own word: it grows much of its own fruit, buys more from growers and makes the wine itself, and the Union des Maisons de Champagne lists it among the houses.

story: Bollinger was founded at Aÿ on 6 February 1829 by three partners, as Renaudin Bollinger: a count who kept his name off the labels, a man of the wine trade, and a young German from Württemberg whose name the house carries. In 1884 it received a Royal Warrant from Queen Victoria (1819 to 1901). The figure every guest has heard of is Elisabeth Bollinger, known as Lily (1899 to 1977), who took charge after her husband's death in 1941, kept the house going through the German occupation, inspected the vineyards by bicycle and led it until 1971. She released R.D. in 1967, a 1952 vintage disgorged late after a long rest on its lees, and in 1969 made the first Vieilles Vignes Françaises, from two small plots of ungrafted Pinot Noir in Aÿ. The house kept old ways that others dropped: fermenting in old oak barrels, holding reserve wines in magnum under cork, riddling and disgorging its vintage wines by hand. Its vintage wine, long sold simply as Bollinger Vintage, took the name Grande Année with the 1976 vintage. In January 2005 Bollinger's holding company bought Ayala, its neighbour in Aÿ.

style.line: Pinot Noir led, broad and vinous: base wines fermented in old oak barrels and reserve wines aged in magnum under cork give toasted brioche, baked apple and a savoury depth.
style.grapes: Pinot Noir leads, chiefly from Aÿ and Verzenay, with Chardonnay from the Côte des Blancs and, in Special Cuvée alone, Meunier; Special Cuvée is over 85 per cent Grand and Premier Cru fruit, by the house.
style.reserve: Special Cuvée holds a majority of reserve wines, by the house's own page, some of them kept in magnum under cork for 7 to 15 years.
style.vessels: Old oak barrels, never new: every base wine of La Grande Année ferments in them, by the house.
style.lees: Special Cuvée ages for twice as long as the appellation requires, by the house; La Grande Année for more than twice the three years required of a vintage wine.
style.dosage: Moderate: 7 to 8 grams a litre for Special Cuvée; 8 for La Grande Année 2012 and 2014 and 6 for the 2018, by the house's pages.

nv.name: Special Cuvée
nv.note: The non vintage Brut: about three fifths Pinot Noir with Chardonnay and Meunier, built on reserve wines, some of them aged in magnum under cork.

cuvee.name: La Grande Année

first.what: The vintage with which the house's vintage wine, sold until then as Bollinger Vintage, took the name Grande Année.

cuvee.rhythm: Made only in the years the house declares. Its own pages show the 2012, 2014, 2015 and 2018 vintages, and the same wine, kept longer, has been the base of R.D. since the 1952 vintage.
cuvee.blend: Pinot Noir, from about three fifths to two thirds, with Chardonnay for the rest; no Meunier.
cuvee.sites: Grand and Premier Cru villages, 19 of them in the 2014 vintage and 11 in the 2015: the Pinot Noir chiefly from Aÿ and Verzenay, the Chardonnay chiefly from Chouilly, with Oiry, Avize or Cuis beside it by the year.
cuvee.making: Every base wine ferments in old oak barrels, never new ones. After blending, the bottles age in the Aÿ cellars under natural cork rather than a crown cap, for more than twice the three years the appellation asks of a vintage wine, and every bottle is riddled and disgorged by hand. The dosage is moderate, 6 to 8 grams a litre by the vintage.
cuvee.lees: More than twice the three years the appellation requires of a vintage wine, in the house's own words; it gives no single figure.
cuvee.young: Baked apple, ripe pear and roasted hazelnut over toasted brioche, with a savoury, almost mushroom depth from the Pinot Noir and the barrels, a firm, vinous body and a fine, steady mousse.
cuvee.aged: Rich enough to pour on release, it grows more savoury and nutty over ten to twenty years; R.D. shows where it goes, the same wine kept far longer on its lees.

forms.name: La Grande Année Rosé
forms.note: The same vintage wine blended with a little still red wine from the house's plot La Côte aux Enfants, in Aÿ.

forms.name: Bollinger R.D.
forms.note: La Grande Année held far longer on its lees and disgorged late; R.D. means recently disgorged, first released in 1967 with the 1952 vintage.

cuvee.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius, never ice cold: the house's own pages give 8 to 10 for the 2014 and 2015 vintages and 10 to 12 for the 2018; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass.

table.house45: Bollinger is the Pinot Noir house of Aÿ, founded in 1829 and named for one of its three founders, a young German from Württemberg. Queen Victoria gave it a Royal Warrant in 1884. The figure guests have heard of is Lily Bollinger, who ran it from 1941 to 1971 and toured the vineyards by bicycle. Bollinger kept old methods that others gave up: it ferments in old oak barrels and ages reserve wines in magnum under cork. That is why the wines taste broad and toasty, with baked apple and roasted hazelnut. Special Cuvée is the one most guests know, and La Grande Année is the vintage wine above it.
table.house10: Bollinger is the Pinot Noir house of Aÿ, founded in 1829: fermented in old oak barrels, rich and toasty, with reserve wines aged in magnum.
table.cuvee45: La Grande Année is the vintage Champagne of Bollinger, made only in years the house declares. Pinot Noir leads it, about three fifths to two thirds, with Chardonnay for the rest. Every base wine ferments in old oak barrels, never new ones, so you get depth without the taste of wood. Then it ages under natural cork for more than six years, and each bottle is riddled and opened by hand. Expect baked apple, roasted hazelnut and toasted brioche, with a savoury, almost mushroom depth. It has the weight for a main course, so I serve it a touch warmer than most Champagne, in a white wine glass.
table.sale: If you want a Champagne with the weight of a white Burgundy, La Grande Année is the one: Pinot Noir led, fermented in old oak barrels and aged for years under cork. Shall I open it with your main course?
table.cuvee10: La Grande Année is Bollinger's vintage Champagne: Pinot Noir led, fermented in old oak barrels and aged under natural cork.
table.cuvee20: La Grande Année is the vintage wine of Bollinger, Pinot Noir led and made only in declared years. It ferments in old oak barrels and ages under natural cork, which gives baked apple, roasted hazelnut and a savoury depth.

guests.q: Does Bollinger make anything above La Grande Année?
guests.a: Two wines stand beside it: R.D., which is La Grande Année kept far longer before it is disgorged, and Vieilles Vignes Françaises, from two small plots of ungrafted Pinot Noir in Aÿ. La Grande Année is the prestige cuvée the class sheet names.
Recently disgorged: it is La Grande Année left on its lees for many more years and disgorged shortly before it is sold, first released in 1967 with the 1952 vintage.
No. The barrels are old and never new, so they give breadth and a savoury note rather than vanilla or the taste of new wood.

guests.q: Why is it called La Grande Année?
guests.a: It means the great year: the house makes it only in the years it declares, and its vintage wine took the name with the 1976 vintage.

traps: The class sheet prints La Grand Année; the label reads La Grande Année, with an e, because année is a feminine word.
R.D. is not a vineyard or a separate blend: it is La Grande Année disgorged years later.
Vieilles Vignes Françaises is ungrafted Pinot Noir from two plots in Aÿ: not old vine Chardonnay, and not the cuvée on the class sheet.
La Grande Année is always a vintage wine; Special Cuvée is the non vintage Brut, and Meunier is in Special Cuvée alone.

sheet.label: La Grande Année
sheet.note: The sheet drops the e of Grande. Année is feminine, so the label reads La Grande Année, the great year; before the 1976 vintage the wine was sold as Bollinger Vintage.

cards.back: La Grande Année, the vintage wine: Pinot Noir led, about three fifths to two thirds, with Chardonnay for the rest.

questions.q: A guest orders the vintage prestige cuvée of the house that Lily Bollinger led from 1941 to 1971. Which wine is it?
questions.exp: La Grande Année is Bollinger's vintage wine. La Grande Dame is Veuve Clicquot's prestige cuvée, Grand Siècle is Laurent-Perrier's blend of several vintages and Grande Cuvée is Krug's multi vintage blend.

questions.q: Which pair of methods sets the Bollinger house style apart, as the house itself describes it?
opts: Old oak barrels and reserve wines in magnum
Stainless steel and no malolactic conversion
Chardonnay alone from the Côte des Blancs
questions.exp: Bollinger ferments its base wines in old oak barrels and keeps reserve wines in magnum under cork for 7 to 15 years. Blocking the malolactic conversion is Gosset's mark, not Bollinger's, and Pinot Noir, not Chardonnay, leads its blends.

questions.q: With which vintage did Bollinger's vintage wine take the name Grande Année?
questions.exp: The wine was sold as Bollinger Vintage until the 1976 vintage, when it became Grande Année. 1952 is the vintage of the first R.D., 1969 the first Vieilles Vignes Françaises and 1829 the year the house was founded.

report: Built on the published flagships record (codex58, key bollinger, refuted on 12 November 2026) and the library's p-bollinger: no fact of either is contradicted.
The service temperature keeps the published record's 9 to 11 degrees Celsius and adds what the house's own pages give by vintage: 8 to 10 for 2014 and 2015, 10 to 12 for 2018.

The villages: the published record says about twenty Grand and Premier Cru villages; the house's pages give 19 crus for the 2014 vintage and 11 for the 2015, so this record gives both by vintage. A refinement, not a contradiction, and listed here so the integrator sees it.

The name: Bollinger Vintage became Grande Année with the 1976 vintage (Decanter and Tastingbook agree). When La was added differs, 1997 by Decanter and 2004 by Tastingbook, so the record does not date it.

The founders' first names differ between accounts, as the published record found, so none is named; 6 February 1829 and the firm's first name, Renaudin Bollinger, are the Union des Maisons de Champagne's.
kind.code: the letters NM were not read on a label. The Union des Maisons de Champagne lists Maison Bollinger among the houses; a refuter should read a label.
style.malolactic is empty: no page read states it. cuvee.bottle is empty: the story of the bottle's shape was not sourced, and the cuvée has no bottle of its own to tell.
The first R.D.: released in 1967 with the 1952 vintage by the house, Decanter and the importer; one Decanter piece dates the style to 1961, which the record leaves out.
More than six years under cork in the spoken line is the house's more than twice the three years the appellation asks, said as a number a guest can keep.
The young glass is the published record's glass, which its refuter left standing; the aged glass is its ageing line.
Whether La Grande Année or Vieilles Vignes Françaises is the prestige cuvée: the class sheet names La Grande Année, and the record answers the guest's question in guests.
